fields.name: Giving to me
fields.meaning: (Someone) gives me N (くださいます: superior; くれます: equal/subordinate)
examples: When I graduated, my teacher gave me a pen.
People from my company gave me flowers on my birthday.
My younger sister gave me a cup for Christmas.
The department manager kindly took me all the way to the station.
The department manager's wife kindly taught me the tea ceremony.
fields.explain:
When a superior gives or presents something to you (or someone close to you), use くださいます.
Combine it with a verb in the te-form to say that someone does something for you.
くださいます can be used for members of the speaker's family.
fields.notes:
explain: ◎ Expresses giving something to someone equal to or below yourself.
examples: 1. あの かばんは 使わなくなったので、妹に やりました。
I don't use that bag anymore, so I gave it to my younger sister.
2. だれかに それを やった んですか。
Who did you give that to?
meaning_vi: Receiving (humble)
explain: Very polite, humble; suitable for emails, announcements, speeches.
Nouns often take the keigo prefix: ご連絡・ご返信・ご協力・お時間・ご厚意.
The tone expresses gratitude; often used with ありがとうございます／感謝する／お礼申し上げる.
“から/より” emphasizes the source; “に” emphasizes the giver (in close conversation).
examples: 1. 先生から参考書をいただきました。
I received a reference book from my teacher.
2. 皆さまから温かいご支援をいただき、心より感謝申し上げます。
We sincerely thank you all for the warm support we have received.
3. 先輩に貴重なご意見をいただいた。
I received valuable advice from a senior colleague.
4. お忙しい中、お時間をいただきありがとうございます。
Thank you for taking the time to see us.
5. 取引先から新しいカタログをいただきました。
We received a new catalog from our business partner.
6. （対比）友だちから本をもらった（casual）／先生から本をいただいた（humble）
Receiving a book from a friend (casual) / from a teacher (humble).
meaning_vi: Giving (a superior gives to me)
explain: Shows respect for the giver; used at work, with customers, superiors, and older people.
Emphasizes gratitude: ～をくださり、ありがとうございます／厚く御礼申し上げます.
“私に” can be omitted if the context makes clear that the recipient is me/my group.
Nouns often take お／ご for extra politeness: ご連絡／ご厚意／お時間をくださる.
examples: 1. 部長が私に最新の資料をくださいました。
The department manager gave me the latest materials.
2. お客様が温かいお言葉をくださった。
The customer gave (us) warm words.
3. 祖父が娘に絵本をくださった。
Grandfather gave a picture book to (my) daughter.
4. 先生がご推薦状をくださいました。
My teacher gave me a letter of recommendation.
5. 田中様がご連絡をくださいました。
Mr./Ms. Tanaka contacted (us).
6. （対比）彼が私に本をくれた（plain）／彼が私に本をくださった（honorific).
Comparing くれる vs くださる.
comparison: Grammar point | Meaning | Difference | Short example
N をくださる | (A superior) gives me | Keigo for くれる | 先生（せんせい）が本（ほん）をくださった
N をくれる | Gives me | Neutral | 友（とも）だちが本（ほん）をくれた
N をいただく | I receive | Humble (receiver's viewpoint) | 先生（せんせい）から本（ほん）をいただいた
N をあげる | I give someone | Giver's viewpoint | 私（わたし）は後輩（こうはい）に資料（しりょう）をあげた
N をさしあげる | Respectfully give | Humble form of あげる | お客（きゃくさま）様（）に試供（しきょう）品（ひん）を差（さ）し上（あ）げる
N をください | Please give me | Request sentence | 名刺（めいし）をください
Vてくださる | (A superior) does V for me | Related verb pattern | ご説明（せつめい）くださる
common_mistakes: • Wrong subject: “私が先生に本をくださる” ×. くださる: the subject must be the giver (the other person); the receiver is me/my group.
• Using くださる with a receiver outside my group: unnatural. Switch to あげる/さしあげる/与える.
• Confusing it with ください (request). ください is not a verb reporting “giving.”
• Omitting the keigo prefix on nouns in polite writing: add ご/お where appropriate.
meaning_vi: Presenting, offering (humble, to a superior)
explain: Highly polite; suitable for receiving guests, ceremonies, business emails.
When the thing given is an abstract act, ご説明／ご案内／ご連絡を差し上げる has a set-formula nuance in business.
When the receiver is not a superior/customer, あげる is enough; using 差し上げる may be too formal.
examples: 1. 私が先生に花束を差し上げました。
I presented a bouquet to my teacher.
2. 後ほど改めてご連絡を差し上げます。
We will contact you again later.
3. お客様に粗品を差し上げております。
We are giving small gifts to our customers.
4. 感謝の気持ちとしてお礼を差し上げます。
Please accept this as a token of our gratitude.
5. 私どもからスケジュール表を差し上げました。
We sent the schedule.
6. （対比）子どもにお菓子をあげる（plain）／先生にお菓子を差し上げる（humble）
comparison: Pattern | Meaning | Difference | Short example
N を差（さ）し上（あ）げる | Respectfully give | Humble form of あげる | 名刺（めいし）を差（さ）し上（あ）げます
N をあげる | Give (plain) | Less formal | 友人（ゆうじん）に花（はな）をあげる
N をくれる | Someone gives me | Receiver's viewpoint | 同僚（どうりょう）が本（ほん）をくれた
N をくださる | (A superior) gives me | Keigo for くれる | 社長（しゃちょう）が資料（しりょう）をくださった
N をいただく | I receive (humble) | Humble, receiver's side | お客（きゃくさま）様（）からご意見（いけん）をいただく
N を進呈（しんてい）する／贈呈（ぞうてい）する | Formal expression | Ceremonial documents | 記念（きねん）品（ひん）を贈呈（ぞうてい）する
Vて差（さ）し上（あ）げる | Do V respectfully for someone | Related verb pattern | ご説明（せつめい）して差（さ）し上（あ）げる × → ご説明（せつめい）いたします／ご説明（せつめい）差（さ）し上（あ）げます
common_mistakes: • Using 差し上げる when the receiver is not a superior/customer: too polite, unnatural in everyday life.
• “ご説明して差し上げる” × (noun + する + 差し上げる overlap). Correct: “ご説明いたします/差し上げます”.
• Confusing viewpoints with くださる/いただく: 差し上げる = I give (humble); くださる = they give (honorific); いただく = I receive (humble).
• Forgetting お／ご with Sino-Japanese nouns in polite writing: ご案内／ご連絡／ご支援 を差し上げる.
meaning_vi: Doing for someone (respectful)
explain: Used with customers/superiors; avoid it with friends/subordinates because it is too formal or mismatches the relationship.
When offering, use ～てさしあげましょうか to politely show you are willing to help.
Avoid excessive humility: consider ご案内します instead of ご案内してさしあげます.
Not used to ask others; to make a request, switch to ～ていただけますか／～ていただきたい。
examples: 1. 荷物をこちらでお預かりしてさしあげます。
We will keep your luggage for you here.
2. 出口までご案内してさしあげます。
I will show you to the exit.
3. よろしければ、資料をコピーしてさしあげましょうか。
If you like, shall I copy the materials for you?
4. 会議の日程は私からご連絡してさしあげます。
I will let you know the meeting schedule.
5. 申し訳ありませんが、その件は対応してさしあげられません。
I'm sorry, but we cannot help you with that matter.
6. 道に迷われたなら、駅まで送ってさしあげます。
If you are lost, I will take you to the station.
comparison: Pattern | Meaning | Difference | Short example
～てさしあげる | Do for someone (humble) | Formal, toward superiors/customers | 説明（せつめい）してさしあげます。
～てあげる | Do for someone (neutral) | Not used with superiors/customers | 手伝（てつだ）ってあげる。
～てやる | Do for someone (blunt/to those below) | Blunt and casual, avoid in formal settings | 犬（いぬ）に水（みず）をやってやる。
お／ご～します | Standard humble form | Concise, natural in business | ご案内（あんない）します。
～ていただく | Have someone do | Receiver's viewpoint | 説明（せつめい）していただく。
common_mistakes: • Wrong relationship (with friends/subordinates). Use ～てあげる instead.
• Making a request with ～てさしあげる: wrong viewpoint; use ～ていただけますか.
• Mixing too much keigo makes it wordy; choose one consistent system (～します/いたします or ～てさしあげる).
• The JLPT often sets up a “customer/superior” context to force the choice of ～てさしあげる or お／ご～します.
meaning_vi: Having (someone) do something for you (humble)
explain: Shows humility on your side; suitable for emails, meetings, services.
When thanking, a clause at the beginning of the sentence is common: ご対応いただき、ありがとうございます。
When making a request, choose a polite question form to avoid sounding like a command: 〜ていただけますか／〜ていただけないでしょうか。
The doer is marked with に/から; it can be omitted if it is clearly the other person.
examples: 1. 先生に推薦状を書いていただいた。
My teacher kindly wrote a letter of recommendation for me.
2. 本日はご出席いただき、誠にありがとうございます。
Thank you very much for attending today.
3. この件、明日までにご連絡いただけますか。
Could you contact us about this matter by tomorrow?
4. 部長にご説明いただきましたので、理解できました。
The department manager explained it to me, so I understood.
5. お忙しいところ、お時間をいただきありがとうございます。
Thank you for taking the time even though you are busy.
6. 先方に日程を調整していただく予定です。
We plan to have the other party adjust the schedule.
comparison: Pattern | Meaning | Difference | Short example
～ていただく | Have something done (humble) | More polite than ～てもらう | 説明（せつめい）していただく
～てもらう | Have something done | Neutral, everyday | 説明（せつめい）してもらう
～てくださる／～てください | A superior does for me / Please do | Honorific viewpoint toward the other person; polite command | 説明（せつめい）してください
～させていただく | Humbly ask to be allowed to do | I do something with permission | 発表（はっぴょう）させていただく
common_mistakes: • Wrong structure: ×説明していただくください → ○説明していただけますか／説明してください.
• Forgetting に/から to mark the doer: ×先生説明していただいた → 先生に説明していただいた.
• Confusing keigo: いただく is humble; くださる is honorific (the other person does it).
• Unnatural doubled keigo: ご説明をしていただきました → ご説明いただきました (concise and correct).
meaning_vi: Table of giving and receiving verbs by level of keigo (さしあげる/やる/いただく/くださる)
examples: 1. わたしは先生に、国のおみやげをさしあげました。
I gave my teacher a souvenir from my country.
2. チンさんは、先生から本をいただいたと言って、喜んでいた。
Chin was happy, saying he had received a book from the teacher.
3. 「きのうはお手紙をいただきまして、ありがとうございました」
“Thank you for the letter you sent me yesterday.”
4. わたしが帰国するとき、先生は新しい辞書をくださいました。
When I returned to my country, my teacher gave me a new dictionary.
5. このお菓子は、兄の上司が（兄に）くださったものだと聞きました。
I heard that these sweets were given (to my older brother) by his boss.
6. 母は毎日花に水をやっている。/ペットの犬にえさをやっている。
My mother waters the flowers every day. / She feeds the pet dog.
7. 「これ、やるよ」「サンキュー」（男性が友だちとの会話で使う）
「Here, this is for you.」「Thanks.」(used by men in conversation with friends)
meaning_vi: when the other person is a superior
when the other person is a subordinate. Animals.
examples: 1. 先生にお茶を入れてさしあげました。
I made tea for my teacher.
2. 「先輩に手伝っていただいたので、いいレポートが書けました」
「My senior helped me, so I was able to write a good report.」
3. お医者様はわたしの質問にていねいに答えてくださいました。
The doctor kindly answered my questions very carefully.
4. 「先生に教えていただいたことは、絶対忘れません」
「I will never forget what you taught me.」
5. 「皆さま、わたしのために、こんなにすばらしいパーティーを開いてくださって、どうもありがとうございました」
「Everyone, thank you so much for throwing such a wonderful party for me.」
6. 今日、久しぶりに犬を洗ってやった。
Today I washed the dog for the first time in a while.
7. 「お父さん、ぼく、サッカーボールがほしいなあ」
「Dad, I want a soccer ball.」
meaning_vi: Doing… for (a subordinate/someone close; a blunt ～てあげる)
meaning_vi: (I) receive N from… (いただきます: from a superior; もらいます: others)
explain: When we receive something from a superior, use いただきます
Combine it with another verb in the te-form to talk about being helped with something.
いただきます can be used for members of the speaker's family.
examples: 1. 私は　社長に　お土産を　いただきました。
I received a souvenir from the company president.
2. 私は　部長に　ワインを　買っていただきました。
The department manager bought me a bottle of wine.
3. 私は　友達に　ケーキを　作ってもらいました。
My friend made a cake for me.
4. 誕生日に　私は　子供に　ピアノを　弾いてもらいました。
On my birthday, my child played the piano for me.
meaning_vi: (I) give N (さしあげます: superior; あげます: equal; やります: subordinate/animals and plants)
explain: さしあげます: Present
あげます: Give (as a gift)
やります: Give
Can be combined with another verb in the te-form to express giving and receiving actions.
あげます is recommended over やります because it is more polite.
examples: 1. 私は　部長に　コーヒーを　さしあげました。
I offered coffee to the department manager.
2. 私は　犬に　えさを　やりました。
I fed the dog.
3. 私は　会社の　人に　ネクタイを　買ってあげました。
I bought a tie for someone at my company.
4. 私は　いもうとに　本を　読んでやりました。
I read a book to my younger sister.
mistakes: Confusing “いただく” (humble) with “くださる” (honoring the giver). Remember: 主語が私＝いただく; 主語が相手＝くださる.
Using “に” instead of “から/より” when you need to emphasize the source formally: prefer から/より.
Adding an unnecessary “する”: ご連絡していただく × (when using the noun + をいただく pattern). Correct: ご連絡をいただく.
Keigo overload: “ご連絡をいただかれました” × (humble + honorific overlap). Stick to one system: いただく or くださる.

fields.name: N1 (person) は N2 (person) に N3を passive verb
fields.meaning: N1 has N3 V-ed by N2 (N1 suffers/receives N2's V)
fields.connection: N1(person)は + N2(person)に + N3を + V passive form
examples: My younger brother broke my computer.
My computer was broken by my younger brother.
I got bitten on the hand by a dog.
fields.explain:
N 2 performs some action on N 3, an object that N 1 owns.
It usually expresses an action that causes trouble for the subject of the sentence.
This form is not used to express appreciation or gratitude.

My friend fixed my computer for me.
私は　友達に　パソコンを　修理されました。　 　　 X
私は　友達に　パソコンを　修理してもらいました。　O
fields.notes: Includes the possessive/indirect passive (足を踏まれた)

fields.name: N1 (person) は N2 (person) に passive verb
fields.connection: N1(person)は + N2(person)に + V passive form
examples: My teacher praised me.
I was praised by my teacher.
My mother asked me to do the shopping.
I was asked by my mother to do the shopping.
I was bitten by a dog.
fields.explain:
N 1 is the topic of the sentence, and N 2, the doer of the action, is marked with the particle に.
The doer of the action (N 2) can be something that moves, such as an animal, a car…

fields.meaning: N1 and N2 are in apposition. The general meaning is “N2, which is N1.”
fields.connection: N1 + の + N2 (apposition: 友達の田中さん)
examples: Beer is made from barley. This is the barley used as the raw material.

fields.name: Ba-form (conditional)
fields.meaning: If… then… (the condition clause uses the ba-form)
fields.connection: V ba-form（Vば / Aければ / Naなら / Nなら） + ～
examples: When autumn comes, the leaves on the trees change color.

A: There's no hot water coming out.
B: If you press this button, hot water will come out.

A: I don't have a ballpoint pen.
B: If you don't have a ballpoint pen, please write in pencil.
fields.explain:
～条件形: If ~
Expresses a condition necessary for something to happen.
Expresses the speaker's judgment in a given situation when the listener says something.
The ba-form is used with verbs, adjectives and nouns.

fields.name: Adjective → adverb
fields.meaning: Turning an adjective into an adverb: Aい→Aく, Na→Naに
examples: I want to become able to whisk tea quickly and skillfully.
fields.explain:
When an adjective modifies a verb, we change the adjective into an adverb as shown above.
早い　→　早く　　上手な　→　上手に

fields.name: V plain form のを 知っていますか
fields.connection: V plain form + のを + 知っていますか
examples:
Did you know that Tanaka quit the company?
No, I didn't know.

Do you know Mr. Miller's address?
No, I don't.
fields.explain:
Used to ask whether the listener knows about a specific piece of information.
If you learned the information through the question, answer 知りませんでした (you did not know before the question, but you know after it).
If you still have no information even after being asked, answer 知りません.

fields.meaning: Vるのが　Aです : Vるの becomes the target described by the adjective A.
examples: I like walking along the beach.
He is good at lying.
fields.explain: This sentence pattern is used with adjectives of liking, disliking and ability, such as すきな、きらいな、じょうずな、へたな、はやい、おそい…

fields.meaning: Vるのは　Aです : Doing V is A.
examples: Watching tennis is interesting.
Memorizing kanji is hard.
fields.explain:
Makes the verb in the dictionary form V る ＋　の the subject of the sentence.
Adjectives often used in this sentence pattern:
むずかしい、やさしい、おもしろい、たのしい、きけんな、たいへんな…

fields.name: Vるのを 忘れました Forgot to V
fields.meaning: Forgot to do… (Vるのを忘れました)
examples: I went shopping, but I forgot to buy eggs.
I forgot to close the car window.
fields.explain: Because忘れました means you have already forgotten, the forgotten action has not happened yet, so V る is always used

fields.meaning: Expresses the state after the change 「知る」.If you don't know, say 「知りません].
fields.connection: 知っていますか → はい、知っています / いいえ、知りません（知っていません is not used）
examples: Do you know? / No, I don't.
Do you know Ms. Hara? No, I don't.
I don't know his plans.

fields.meaning: ちからず expresses things that have no exceptions, predictions close to reality, strong will, or calls and urging to act.
fields.connection: 必ず/きっと + V（strong affirmative） / ぜひ + Vたい・Vてください
examples: I always brush my teeth after meals.
We're definitely going to win tomorrow's match!
You'll surely get a good score on the next test.

Tom: “Please come visit my country by all means.”
Yamada: “Yes, I'd really love to go.”

fields.meaning: Indicates a way of doing something with a demonstrative: do it like this/like that/like that over there (こう/そう/ああ+V)
examples: (At a dance class)「Look. If you do it like this, it looks beautiful.」
「Mr. Yamada may not look it, but he's still only in his fifties.」
「Please be sure to call when you'll be late.」「Okay, I will.」
This problem isn't that difficult.
Do you like him that much?
It's not that hot today, is it?
I'm not that hungry, so just a little is fine.
It's not as if I have that much time.
If you're going to say that much, go ahead and try it.
fields.explain:
Softening negative: そんなに〜ない → polite, modest, avoids sounding blunt.
In questions it expresses surprise or doubt: そんなに？/そんなにするの？
When used for strong emphasis in the affirmative, it can carry a nuance of criticism: そんなに怒らなくてもいい。
Often appears in conversation, responding to the other person's opinion.

• Indicates degree/size “to that extent / like that” compared with an implied standard (the situation mentioned or the listener's side).
• Often used with the negative to soften: そんなに忙しくない (not that busy).
• Used in questions to confirm/express doubt: そんなに痛い？ (does it hurt that much?).
• Compared with それほど: そんなに is colloquial and based on the “standard” of the listener/the topic just mentioned; それほど is more neutral.
fields.notes:
• “そんなに？” on its own in conversation expresses doubt/encourages the speaker to explain more.
• In business emails, それほど is often more natural than そんなに to stay neutral.
• With quantities: そんなに多くはない／そんなに時間がない。
mistakes: Confusing it with “そんな + N” (kind) → “そんなに + Adj/V” (degree).
Using “とても～ない” (incorrect) instead of “そんなに～ない”: they have different functions.
Forgetting the negative when you mean “not to that extent”: × そんなに難しい → ○ そんなに難しくない (when you want to soften).

fields.meaning: Used to state a consequence of what was mentioned before (a fact, a judgment, a request).
examples: These are 100 yen each. So three of them are 300 yen.
It's already 8 p.m. So I think there's nobody in the classroom.
People walk through here a lot. So don't leave things here.
What kind of movies do you like?
What does that mean?
What did you mean by what you said yesterday?
How do you say this word in English?
What do you mean you're suddenly not coming?
How should I set it up?
fields.explain:
Used when you want the listener to define/describe something clearly and specifically; suitable for Q&A, meetings, classes.
Intonation determines politeness: どういう意味でしょうか (polite) vs どういうつもり？ (harsh).
In emails/minutes, use どのような instead of どういう to be formal.

• “どういう～” asks about the kind, nature, specific content, or the intention/meaning of a preceding word/sentence.
• The tone can be neutral (asking for information) or carry a nuance of interrogation, demanding an explanation, depending on context/intonation.
• Compared with どんな: どういう usually asks for more factual information/a specific definition, and is less subjective.
• “どういうこと？” is stronger than “どういう意味？”; the latter focuses on the meaning of a word/sentence, the former on the situation/matter.
fields.notes:
• “どういうことだ” at the end of a sentence can be an exclamation of indignation/surprise: 一体どういうことだ！
• “どういう風の吹き回しで” is a set phrase: “what wind has blown you here (why are things like this today)”.
• “どういう経緯で” asks about the background and course of events leading to a result.
mistakes: Confusing どういう with どれ（which one）/どの（which N）: どういう asks about kind/meaning, not a choice.
Using どういう in formal writing: replace it with どのような to be safe in JLPT reading/writing.
“どういうこと？” easily sounds confrontational; on the JLPT, pay attention to the context so you don't take it as a purely informational question.
